title-group.article-title: A Single Public Lidar Data Model for Cross-Border Archaeology and Its Research Potential: A Case Study into Roman Land Division and Agricultural Use in Istria, Croatia

abstract.p: Publicly available airborne laser scanning (ALS) data offers considerable potential for archaeological research, yet remains extending across modern borders are often divided among national and regional datasets. This paper presents a cross-border approach to ALS data from Croatia, Slovenia and the Italian region of Friuli Venezia Giulia. The datasets were harmonised, rasterised at a resolution of 0.5 m and integrated into a single Web Map Service designed for archaeological interpretation. This integrated dataset has significant research potential, as demonstrated by a case study of Roman land division across the Gulf of Trieste and the Istrian Peninsula, which covers an area of approx. 4000 km2. At a macro level, the analysis identifies four distinct land divisions, suggesting their boundaries and their landscape context. Examining these systems within a continuous geographical framework allows for a fresh perspective on Roman territorial organisation. At a finer scale, the study focuses on patterns of subdivision within individual centuriae. ALS data enable a more detailed analysis of Roman land use, offering a new interpretation of these subdivisions. Thus, the study demonstrates how harmonised, cross-border ALS data can connect broader questions of Roman territorial organisation with a detailed analysis of the physical remains.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: The history of archaeological remote sensing in Croatia spans eight decades. The use of vertical aerial photographs for archaeological research by John Bradford, who served with the Royal Air Force Air Photography and Reconnaissance Unit in Puglia, Italy, towards the end of the Second World War, is closely associated with this field [1]. This allowed for the first time a panoramic view of the remains of Roman land surveying in the countries around the Mediterranean Sea. He initiated large-scale research into the subject, thereby sparking a competition to publish the first findings on Roman surveying along the eastern Adriatic coast (e.g., [2]). To this day, a close connection remains between aerial archaeology and research into Roman surveying, not only in Croatia but throughout Europe.

The introduction of airborne laser scanning (ALS, lidar) in Croatian archaeology, which occurred almost 15 years ago, has precipitated a comparable revolution to that initiated by Bradford in the field of aerial archaeology. This was primarily because ALS allowed for the exploration of areas that were previously inaccessible to other prospection methods. However, the limited use of ALS methodology in Croatian archaeology over the past decade can be attributed to the fact that, prior to 2024, such investigations were only feasible using project-specific data. This is also reflected in the limited number of publications in comparison to neighbouring regions in Slovenia and Italy. This situation has changed after 2024, when the data from the ALS survey of Croatia became publicly available upon request [3].

ALS data have a wide range of potential applications in Croatian archaeology, with the mapping of selected archaeological features and new sites being the most common (e.g., [4]). The method also yields good results, particularly for long linear features such as traces of Roman land surveying (e.g., [5,6,7,8,9]) or the remains of military camps [10]. However, ALS is also a powerful data source that can deliver encouraging results, particularly in the context of landscape-based archaeological research [11]. ALS data can provide insight into the interaction between human settlements and the natural environment, helping us to understand how natural terrain has been used or modified to meet human needs [12]. Furthermore, it is possible to combine underwater and terrestrial research, which is particularly relevant in coastal areas due to rising sea levels [13]. Deriving relative stratigraphic information from ALS data is a key aspect, as this often provides fundamental initial insight into the temporal development and change of a regional landscape [14].

The examples above demonstrate the significant benefits of the ALS method. As with any technique, it has its advantages and disadvantages, and it achieves the best results when used alongside other prospection methods. To ensure optimal use of the data, it is also essential to be aware of the parameters involved in the ALS data acquisition, processing and visualisation (e.g., [15,16,17]). The same applies to the publicly available ALS data for Croatia. Although this dataset is of excellent quality, it has been processed for general, versatile applications. This means that certain limitations must be accepted when using it for archaeological purposes.

Firstly, the result is a visualisation of a digital terrain model (DTM) which has already been pre-classified according to general criteria. This is not ideal for archaeological purposes, since dry stone walls, ruins, and buildings have been removed from the data. Secondly, it is currently not possible to load the terrain model or its visualisation directly as a Web Map Service layer into a geographic information system, such as QGIS. Thirdly, most archaeological studies end at national borders because ALS data does not extend beyond them.

In this context, the archaeological study of remains of Roman land division in Istria presented here serves as an example. Our focus is on the area stretching across Croatia, Slovenia and the Italian region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia. Our aim is twofold: first, to determine whether the limitations of publicly accessible ALS data for archaeological studies can be overcome and, second, to explore the advantages of large-scale data interpretation. The results are analysed at both the macro and micro scales. Roman land surveying (centuriatio) is a supra-regional event (macro scale), while evidence of the internal division of survey units (centuriae) has only been preserved within local areas (micro scale).

The paper is organised into five main sections. Section 1 provides the introduction, which establishes the research context, objectives, and significance of publicly available airborne laser scanning data and presents the Istrian study area. Section 2 describes the airborne laser scanning data used in the study, explains how they were harmonised into a cross-border digital feature model and archaeological visualisation and outlines the interpretative methods used to identify and reconstruct Roman land divisions and associated land use features. Section 3 presents the results at macro and micro scales. Section 4 discusses the archaeological, geographical, historical, and methodological implications of these findings, together with the strengths and limitations of the approach. The conclusion summarises the principal results, methodological contribution, and priorities for future research.

sec.title: 1.1. Geographical Context
sec.p: Istria is the largest peninsula of the Adriatic Sea, extending southward between the Gulf of Trieste and the Kvarner Gulf. Most of the peninsula lies within Croatia, while its northern part includes areas of Slovenia and a small portion of Italy near Trieste. Its shape is roughly triangular, with a varied coastline of bays, headlands, small islands, and sheltered harbours. The western coast is generally lower, more accessible, and more deeply indented, with many coastal towns. By contrast, the eastern coast is steeper and more rugged, where hillsides descend sharply toward the waters of the Kvarner Gulf. Istria’s lithology is varied and traditionally divided into three main zones, commonly known as White, Grey, and Red Istria. White Istria, in the northeast, is the highest and most mountainous part of the peninsula and is composed mostly of limestone. The highest ground along the narrow Učka ridge forms a clear natural barrier between Istria and the neighbouring mainland. Grey Istria, in the central interior, takes its name from the impermeable flysch deposits. This zone contains permanent rivers, including Mirna, Dragonja, and Raša. Red Istria covers most of the peninsula and consists of a limestone plateau covered by distinctive red soil. The limestone areas are defined by typical karst landforms, including sinkholes, caves, and subterranean drainage systems. The climate is primarily Mediterranean along the coast, with dry summers and mild winters, while the interior is cooler and wetter. Vineyards, olive groves, forests, and pasturelands contribute to Istria’s varied physical character [18,19,20].

sec.title: 1.2. Historical Background
sec.p: The region came under Roman influence in the late 3rd century BC; this was followed by over 200 years of armed conflict on the eastern Adriatic coast and in the hinterland [21]. It was only from the time of Caesar that the Roman expansionist policy was able to initiate long-term processes such as urbanisation, land surveying and infrastructure development, including the rise of the two Istrian colonies of Parentium and Pola [22]. The years of Augustus’s reign led to Italy becoming its final ancient border, and the division into 11 regions also brought economic changes for the Istrian Peninsula (Regio X Venetia et Histria). Following the establishment of Regio X, which included parts of modern-day Croatia and Slovenia, the river Formio (Rižana) came to form the northern boundary of Histria [23]. This was subsequently changed when the River Raša took its place.

Research on Roman monuments, epigraphic, written and archaeological sources provide a detailed picture of the Roman presence [24,25,26]. Alongside studies on Roman centuriatio (e.g., [9,27]), numerous studies have centred on grand coastal Roman estates (villae maritimae), renowned for their opulent architecture and decorative elements (e.g., [28,29]). The construction of the villae maritimae was closely linked to the so-called maritime infrastructure (pier, breakwater, landing stage, etc.), which is now submerged due to the sea level rising since Roman times [30]. The contribution of underwater archaeology indicates that about 70% of the villae maritimae were provided with structures related to maritime traffic [general overview in 31 with older literature]. Submerged infrastructure remains are primarily evaluated in the context of the transport of products and their economic or hierarchical role in the context of maritime connectivity [24,31].

However, the backbone of the Roman economy, seen over the centuries of Roman rule, was formed by more than 200 small villae rusticae, which offer numerous references to the production of wine or olive oil [26]. The widespread and massive diffusion of Istrian olive oil, together with the praise of its qualities by Pliny the Elder and Martial [26], attest to the practice of large-scale, systematic olive cultivation and agriculture in Histria. This high level of production must have remained widespread until at least the 3rd century AD, when African exports largely replaced Istrian products on the market [32,33]. Still, no physical remains of Roman olive groves have been found in Istria to date. This may be due to the lack of evidence. However, it may also be caused by the fact that the remains of land use have rarely been the subject of research to date, and when studied, the focus has been exclusively on Roman land division.

The study of the centuriatio, i.e., the regular division of land into square plots of 20 × 20 actus (approx. 710 × 710 m), is the most discussed and researched element of land use in Istria. The limites or boundaries of the land division could be marked by stones or defined by roads, paths, ditches, hedges, dry stone walls, or other features. Their remains were already recognised from terrestrial observation by P. Kandler [34], but it was another 100 years before J. Bradford [1] observed them from an aerial perspective. Topographical maps, aerial photographs and terrestrial observations were, for the following decades, the basis for research on the Roman centuriatio system of Pola and Parentium [2,27,35]. Later, investigations were also enabled by the availability of satellite images and with the advent of ALS when highly eroded topographic structures (e.g., remains of dry stone walls) became visible even under dense vegetation [9,36].

At the same time, the integrated interpretation of large-scale remote sensing data has provided the first solid evidence of Roman agriculture in the area surrounding Medulin Bay and on the island of Veli Brijun [37]. Of particular interest in the Medulin Bay area are the planting pits, which are sometimes combined with dry stone walls arranged in a regular grid pattern covering a minimum area of at least 13 hectares. They most probably represent the remains of orchards or (tree) nurseries bordering the villa maritima in Močile Bay. The same type of small-scale parcelling was also confirmed in the area of the villa maritima in Verige Bay.

sec.title: 2.1. ALS Datasets
sec.p: Three ALS datasets were used in this study: the Croatian national ALS survey, the Slovenian national ALS survey, and the ALS survey from Friuli-Venezia Giulia (FVG), Italy. Their individual characteristics and processing procedures are described in the following subsections, along with the approach used to merge them into the combined dataset (CFVGS-CVAT). The data differ in terms of how they are collected and processed. It was therefore a key priority to harmonise the data first and then merge them in a second step (Figure 1).

sec.title: 2.1.1. Croatia
sec.p: Data for the Croatian national ALS survey was acquired in 2022 and 2023 for the purpose of disaster risk reduction assessment. Rasterised DTM and DSM at 1 m spatial resolution as well as classified point cloud data are available free of charge, but a formal request is required to access them [3]. The license permits free unlimited reuse and reproduction but limits distribution and publication in a form that does not disclose individual coordinates and the heights of objects. This means that visualisations may be shared with third parties; however, the elevation models themselves may not.

Each data tile covers a bit less than 1 km2 and is organised within a 1200 × 800 m2 grid. The dataset covers the entire national territory, including the islands, except for areas along the border with Serbia, where data were not acquired (Figure 1). Data acquisition specifications are available [41,42], but the Croatian State Geodetic Administration (DGU) does not release the technical details of the actual scanning parameters or quality control. The specified minimum scanning density was 4 pts/m2 in rural and forested areas (about 70% of the territory) and 8 pts/m2 in urban areas (30% of the territory) [42]. A special survey was done along 4100 km of major river corridors with a specified point density of 20 pts/m2 [41]. The aggregate point density for the whole scanned area, on average (22.0 pts/m2), exceeds these requirements (Table 1).

The rasterised elevation models from DGU are complete for the whole scanned territory of Croatia, but the point clouds for 12 tiles east of Zagreb contain voids along a narrow strip (30–160 m wide) in the extreme eastern part of each tile (Supplementary Materials S1). We interpolated the voids up to 50 m wide, but the interpolated areas do not contain meaningful data and therefore have a negative effect on archaeological interpretation. Ground points in one tile in the east of the country are in the wrong class (3—low vegetation) (Supplementary Materials S2) and we therefore changed the classification into class 2 (ground) before rasterisation.

sec.title: 2.1.2. Italy—Friuli-Venezia Giulia (FVG)
sec.p: ALS data for the whole territory of the Autonomous Region of Friuli-Venezia Giulia (FVG) were acquired between 2017 and 2020. The specified minimum scanning density was very high at 10 pls/m2 for mountainous areas with elevation above 1000 m and 16 pls/m2 for lower elevations [43]. Data properties of the survey are shown in Table 1.

The classified point clouds are tiled in a 388.4 × 555.6 m2 grid, while the DTM, DSM, and digital feature model (DFM) with 0.5 m resolution are tiled in a 900 × 840 m2 nonuniform grid. All products are provided at ellipsoidal and orthometric heights [44]. A compressed DTM hillshading can be downloaded for the whole region in a single file. Data are licensed under Italian Open Data License v2.0 [45] and can be used, modified, redistributed, and commercialised freely, provided that the source is cited, and official endorsement is not implied.

Although the data are freely and openly available, the download process is impractical for larger areas. For access to the complete dataset, it is therefore preferable to contact the regional authorities directly.

The rasterised elevation models of FVG cover the entire scanned territory. However, the point clouds for 554 tiles, mostly in the mountainous north-west, contain voids (Supplementary Materials S3). For these areas, we used the precomputed DFMs.

sec.title: 2.1.3. Slovenia
sec.p: The second ALS survey of the whole Slovenian territory took place in 2023–2025 as part of the first cyclical laser scanning campaign. Technical specifications for the survey were published as a part of the tender [46]. The quality control documents for all twelve survey blocks, classified point cloud data, as well as DTM, digital surface model (DSM), normalised digital surface model (nDSM), and hillshading at 0.5 m resolution are available without registration [47] and are distributed under a CC BY 4.0 licence. Beyond the entire territory of Slovenia, a buffer zone of varying width (0.3–4.5 km) was identified, extending into neighbouring countries.

Data is organised in a 1 × 1 km2 grid; however, point cloud datasets often include some points outside the tile boundaries. Up to ten tiles can be downloaded at once, although this limit is not strictly enforced. Larger data volumes must be ordered from the Slovenian Surveying and Mapping Authority. The specified aggregate nominal point density was 10 pts/m2, but the actual average density was considerably higher, at 36.2 pts/m2 (Table 1).

sec.title: 2.1.4. Combined Croatia–Friuli-Venezia Giulia–Slovenia Dataset (CFVGS-CVAT)
sec.p: Our aim was to harmonise the data as far as possible without reclassifying the ALS point cloud data. The goal was to produce a combined 0.5 m resolution visualisation of digital feature models (DFM) that archaeologists and others interested in terrain morphology and surface features can use freely, easily, and comparably, without additional data processing.

For all three data acquisition projects, laser scanners operating at a 1064 nm wavelength were used. As shown in Table 1, the three datasets differ in pulse density, point density and density of points classified as ground and buildings. The minimum scanning densities specified in technical documentation are typically expressed as aggregate points (returns) per square meter (pts/m2) and provide only an approximate indication of the densities in the final point clouds. However, point density alone is not an adequate metric, as data acquired under in-leaf conditions may yield a large proportion of returns from above-ground vegetation rather than the terrain surface. A more relevant metric for archaeological prospection is aggregate pulse density (pls/m2), especially density of ground points (ground pts/m2), which are used to compute a digital terrain model (DTM) or density of returns from ground and buildings, which are used to compute a digital feature model (DFM). A case in point are the three datasets used in this study. The aggregate pulse and point densities are much higher for FVG than for Slovenia and Croatia, but this is not reflected in the quality of the DFM, as the density of returns classified as ground or buildings is the lowest (Table 2, Figure 2). This is because many of the returns are within vegetation or remain unclassified. However, it also does not imply that the lower ground-return density in the FVG dataset means a lower DFM quality at 0.5 m resolution or reduced archaeological feature detectability, because all three datasets have relatively high densities of returns classified as ground or buildings. The densities differ between the three datasets; however, spatial variability within each dataset is greater than the differences between their aggregate densities.

As mentioned in the Introduction, a DTM is not ideal for archaeological purposes. It is a model of the bare ground that is free of anthropogenic and natural objects, for example, buildings, bridges and vegetation. Built, especially protruding archaeological structures that are not part of the terrain are therefore filtered out by definition [48]. Therefore, a so-called digital feature model (DFM) has proven advantageous in archaeology in recent years because it combines the terrain with buildings and other structures that may have been classified as such [49]. A specific, multi-step classification procedure can be used to classify points and rasterise them into a DFM [50]. However, applying such a procedure at national or supra-national scale is a major undertaking, and the process is also more suited for low density datasets. For this reason, we rasterised a DFM for each country from points that have already been classified as ground and buildings, corresponding to classes 2 and 6 in the ASPRS LAS specification [51]. The technical reports for the Slovenian ALS survey (e.g., [52]) very briefly describe the classification process as a mixture of automatic and manual procedures using RiProcess, Terrasolid, LAStools and “AI”. However, they provide no detail on the exact methods or parameters used. We could find no available reference on the classification methods used by data providers for Croatia and FVG. We rasterised the point clouds with blast2dem and las2dem tools [53], which use Delaunay triangulation followed by linear interpolation over a Triangulated Irregular Network (TIN) [54]. All point-to-point gaps smaller than 100 m were filled.

All three datasets have a high aggregate density of returns classified as ground or buildings (Table 1), sufficient for rasterisation into a 0.5 m resolution DFM. The common spatial resolution ensures consistent raster sampling and application of visualisation parameters across the three datasets but does not imply uniform archaeological resolving power. The effective visibility and detectability of archaeological features depend on the scanning density, vegetation conditions during acquisition, point classification, and consequently the distribution of ground returns, terrain morphology, and the dimensions and preservation of individual features. Spatial variability of ground point density is important to consider because some regions in all three countries were scanned in leaf-on conditions and these areas remain difficult to prospect for archaeological features [55], because lower density of ground returns can mean interpolation across larger gaps between observations, less reliable representation of small or low-relief archaeological features, and their reduced detectability. The density map in Figure 2 provides a regional overview of the spatial variability of ground and building returns at the scale of the original ALS tiles. This allows users to identify broader spatial differences in the characteristics of the source datasets and easily identify areas where scanning conditions, especially the date of scanning, were not optimal. Although finer-resolution density maps could provide additional information for assessing the local suitability of ALS data for archaeological interpretation, their production at the scale of the combined dataset falls beyond the scope of this study.

The three ALS datasets use ellipsoidal heights referenced to different national realizations of ETRS89. To assess their vertical consistency, we compared DFM elevations over a smooth, stable surface (a section of highway). The observed height differences ranged from 0.06 to 0.12 m between the Slovenia—FVG data and from 0.06 to 0.15 m between the Slovenia—Croatia data. These differences are small and comparable to the vertical accuracy commonly specified for ALS-derived elevation models (approximately 0.10–0.15 m). Furthermore, the combined dataset was produced by merging visualisations computed separately from the national DFMs, rather than merging the elevation models themselves. Consequently, the observed height differences do not introduce artificial elevation discontinuities into the combined product and do not affect its validity or interpretability.

The currently available visualisation products for all three ALS datasets are hillshaded DTMs. For Croatia, a 1 m resolution hillshade is available as a base layer on the Geoportal DGU [56]. For FVG, a 0.5 m resolution hillshade can be downloaded [44], while for Slovenia a 0.5 m resolution hillshade is available for download and as a WMS base layer [47,57]. In addition, a 0.5 m resolution visualisation for archaeological topography (VAT) is available for Slovenia as a WMS base layer, but only for data from 2011 to 2015 [57].

Hillshading is a standard visualisation whose advantage is its instant legibility. It is typically calculated with a light source in the north-west [16]. However, it has the disadvantage that linear features that lie in the direction of the light source cast no shadow and therefore become less distinct or even invisible. This can have a particularly negative impact on interpretation of the linear patterns, which are characteristic of Roman surveying. Furthermore, structures with only very subtle topographical expressions are difficult to discern.

A range of visualisations has been developed specifically for archaeological research (e.g., [17,48,49,58,59,60,61,62,63]). Of particular interest is the Combined Visualisation for Archaeological Topography (CVAT), which blends four visualisation methods—hillshade, slope, positive openness, and sky-view factor—computed with varied predetermined settings into a single image. It is therefore especially well-suited to support interpretation of archaeological traces in lidar-derived elevation models. CVAT can enhance the visibility of features that differ in scale, height, orientation, and form, across terrain from very flat to very steep. Kokalj [48] provides a detailed comparison of visualisation methods used in ancient Maya lidar research and outlines best practices for computing and publishing ALS-derived images, including metadata requirements, recommendations for reproducible workflows, and the rationale for proposing CVAT as a suitable base visualisation.

Based on these considerations, we used Relief Visualisation Toolbox Python (v.2.2.2) library (rvt-py, [64]) to compute CVAT with default settings ([48] Supporting Information), for all three DFMs at 0.5 m resolution. The resulting visualisations were mosaicked into a single file in a common projection, ETRS89/UTM zone 33N (ETRS 25833). Bilinear interpolation was used for resampling. As the Slovenian dataset overlaps both neighbouring datasets, we defined the mosaic seamlines along the Slovenian national boundary with a 10 m outward buffer. The datasets were mosaicked along these seamlines without feathering or blending. The data are available openly and freely as a WMTS service [65].

sec.title: 2.2. Methods of Interpretation
sec.p: The study area covers more than 4000 km2. Based on the research question and the size of the area to be mapped, instead of a thorough diachronic interpretation, a targeted interpretative approach was adopted, focusing on Roman land divisions (centuriatio), their internal subdivisions and the potential use of land plots.

Data interpretation is based on the ALS-derived digital feature models (DFMs) presented above and their combined visualisation for archaeological topography (CVAT). Additionally, features were interpreted from the Croatian digital orthophoto map which was produced from vertical aerial photographs taken between 1950 and 1968 [66]. According to the documentation, most of the photographs taken over Istria were acquired in 1968. The photographs of the study area were therefore taken a bit more than two decades after the wartime photographs that Bradford had at hand to conduct his research. The vertical photograph published on Plate 41 [1] shows parts of the Roman land division in the east of Istria marked by dry stone walls and a systematic layout of stone piles. The photographed area differs only slightly from the 1968 images. Differences are particularly evident in the vegetation. However, the archaeological information is of equal value. The more significant changes to the landscape resulting from the construction of new settlements and roads therefore did not take place until after 1968. Therefore, we could use the black-and-white photographs of the digital orthophoto map for interpreting today’s lost archaeological remains. The tiles of the orthophotomap are of excellent quality and were especially helpful in mapping the stone piles (see Section 3).

During the interpretation process, Roman land division systems were identified through a visual analysis of the dry stone walls preserved within the DFM as linear landscape features. The criteria for distinguishing the original limites from later dry stone walls were informed by previous fieldwork in the municipality of Vrsar, north of Lim Canal and within the Istrian land division (Grid 2), published in 2021 [9]. This fieldwork compared their physical forms in the field with their appearance in ALS data. In the field, the original limites often have no clearly recognisable wall form and may survive as low piles or scattered stones, with only slight local differences in ground level. Their continuity as long linear features is generally difficult to follow on the ground. In ALS, however, they appear as flattened, undulating linear features of positive relief, making their continuity traceable over much longer distances. Later walls remain recognisable in the field as built walls, even when partially dilapidated. In ALS, their faces produce a sharper, more clearly defined linear signature. The Vrsar fieldwork predates the present study; the understanding gained during this study informed interpretation across the wider study area, where the same morphological expression of the original limites is visible in ALS data.

All features interpreted as limites during the visual analysis were vectorised in GIS. The grids were then reconstructed from these mapped features, taking into account their spatial arrangement, morphology and the standard dimensions of a Roman centuria (20 × 20 actus). After reconstructing the grids, we reviewed the ALS data again, paying particular attention to apparent gaps. Some limites are sufficiently faint to require close inspection at high magnification, when only a small portion of the landscape is visible. Across such an extensive study area, moving between these detailed views makes it difficult to maintain an overview of coverage, and some remains may consequently be overlooked. The projected axes provided a spatial reference for this subsequent examination. The additional limites identified during this review met the same morphological criteria as those mapped initially and supplemented the existing evidence without changing the reconstructed extent or interpretation of the land divisions.

Post-Roman and more recent dry stone walls that follow the course of the Roman cadastre have also been documented. This enables the percentage of surviving Roman dry stone walls as part of younger field systems to be determined. For the northern Adriatic islands of Cres and Krk, for example, this figure is estimated to be between 10 and 15% [8]. As many of the numerous stone piles in the study area on the east coast of Istria are thought to be of Roman origin [67], these remains were also included in the analysis of Roman land use. Many of them have disappeared in recent decades and are therefore visible in historical orthophoto but are not present in the DFM anymore. This is due to their removal as part of modern land use for urban development or agriculture.

The subsequent reconstruction of the survey grids was carried out in two different ways, as the first line of enquiry focused on large-scale survey grid patterns, whilst the second concerned the detailed aspects of the use of the individual centuriae. The reconstructed extent of the identified large-scale land division systems was initially defined by the distribution of the outermost preserved limites that could be securely assigned to each grid. Based on selecting the best-preserved cardo or decumanus as a reference line, different grid sizes were tested, resulting in the generation of offsets across the landscape.

For computation of the orientation of each grid, all lines were first split at their vertices. Because the computed orientation should be independent of the direction in which a line was drawn—for example, left to right should be equivalent to right to left—we converted all orientations to the range of 0–180° using modulo 180°. We then treated the orientations as circular data and weighed all averages by the actual segment length in metres. For each Grid, we first collapsed perpendicular orientations onto a 90° cycle, using modulo 90°, estimated the length-weighted grid axis, and calculated its circular standard deviation. A small number of digitised segments do not strictly follow the predominant grid orientation but were nevertheless included in the dataset because they were interpreted as being of Roman origin and associated with the respective land division. To prevent these deviations from influencing the estimated grid orientation, we excluded segments deviating by more than 3 circular SD from the final calculation. The threshold provides a practical criterion for distinguishing the predominant grid alignment from local deviations without excluding minor variations. Importantly, these segments were retained in the archaeological dataset and excluded only from the final statistical calculation of grid orientation. Because these segments are generally short, they have negligible effect on the combined orientation—the average remains the same for all four grids. Nevertheless, the identified outliers can be easily screened for potential misinterpretations. The calculations of orientations were done in QGIS in ETRS 1989 UTM zone 33N (EPSG 25833) projection. Python code that can be directly added to QGIS as an easily executable processing script is included in the Supplementary Material.

In comparison, the micro case study area on the east coast of Istria is relatively small, with 50 km2, but it exhibits an exceptionally high density of Roman dry stone walls. This is why it is of interest when considering the use of the individual centuriae. The micro scale study area forms part of the main Istrian surveying grid (Grid 2, see Section 3), even though local adaptations to the terrain are noticeable. These differences are discussed in detail in the following section.

sec.title: 3.1. Roman Land Division Across the Gulf of Trieste and Istria: A Regional Perspective
sec.p: The integrated, transnational ALS dataset enables the study of areas spanning over 4000 km2 and Roman land divisions across the Gulf of Trieste and the Istrian Peninsula within a single geographical framework. This approach transcends the limitations of modern national boundaries and datasets. Altogether, four land divisions were identified, with their proposed extents shown in Figure 3 and numerical data on the identified grid lines and their orientations presented in Table 3.

sec.title: 3.1.1. Tergeste Land Division (Grid 1)
sec.p: Previous ALS studies identified parts of the Tergeste land division on both sides of the present-day Italian–Slovenian border. Mlekuž [68] mapped numerous linear features on the Slovenian Kras and reconstructed their corresponding land division grid. Independently, Bernardini [69] documented further evidence in the southern Trieste Karst, including rural estates whose enclosure walls he interpreted as aligned with one of the axes of the same land division. The integrated ALS dataset allows this previously documented evidence to be examined together with newly identified limites in the coastal area of Friuli-Venezia Giulia, demonstrating that they form part of a single land division system extending across the modern border (Figure 4). Based on the orientation and spacing of identified features, a cadastral grid composed of centuriae measuring 706 × 706 m was reconstructed in a GIS environment. The reconstructed grid has an orientation of 41.6°. Limites identified throughout the study area conform closely to this grid.

The best preserved remains occur in several distinct areas. In the vicinity of Trieste, limites survive at Monte Calvo and Padriciano. Additional centuriae and boundary features occur north-west of Sežana, between Gorjansko and Komen, and in the vicinity of Temnica on the Slovenian Kras. Along the Friuli-Venezia Giulia coastline, limites were identified between Santa Croce and Sistiana.

The south-easternmost remains of the grid occur in the vicinity of Loka. At its north-western end, a possible limes was identified near Monfalcone. As this feature is isolated and not associated with other elements of the land division, its interpretation remains uncertain. If excluded, the north-westernmost securely identified remains are those preserved near Temnica.

sec.title: 3.1.2. Istrian Land Division (Grid 2)
sec.p: The Roman centuriatio of Istria has been studied since the mid-nineteenth century and represents one of the best-known examples of Roman land division on the eastern Adriatic coast [2,9,27,34,35,70]. Earlier reconstructions relied primarily on modern cadastral parcels, roads, and field boundaries that retained the orientation and spacing of the land division grid. The land division associated with Pola and Parentium was therefore reconstructed largely from the persistence of its geometric layout in the modern landscape, while original built limites were only rarely distinguished from later boundaries and directly documented.

ALS data fundamentally change this situation by allowing preserved built limites to be identified and mapped as discrete topographic features (Figure 5). The potential of this approach was first demonstrated in the municipality of Vrsar, where ALS interpretation, GIS analysis, field survey, and archaeological excavation confirmed the survival of Roman limites within the modern landscape [9]. National ALS coverage now makes it possible to apply the same approach across the entire peninsula.

The main Istrian land division (Grid 2) is the largest and best-preserved of the four systems examined here. Based on the distribution and orientation of the identified limites, a cadastral grid composed of centuriae measuring approximately 706 × 706 m was reconstructed in a GIS environment. Repeated parallel offsets nevertheless produced a slightly closer fit with a module of approximately 706 × 707 m, with the spacing between successive decumani closer to 707 m. The implications of this minor discrepancy for the original surveying process are beyond the scope of the present study. The grid has an orientation of 17.9°. The identified limites conform closely to this reconstruction, allowing the system to be traced from the Pomer–Medulin area in southern Istria to the Dragonja River. No limites attributable to this land division were identified east of a line running through the areas of Rakalj, Svetvinčenat, Sveti Petar u Šumi, Tićan, and Vižintini.

The land division is most clearly materialised in the southern part of the peninsula, where a dense network of original limites is complemented by modern roads and property boundaries that retain the orientation of the Roman survey. Farther north, the built realisation of the grid follows a more discontinuous pattern. In the hinterland of Rovinj, a dense concentration of built structures extends from Mulem to Bubani within a strip of exactly five centuriae wide. By contrast, in the hinterland of Poreč, a strip of the same width extending from Dračevac to Milanezi contains no built limites. The boundaries of these sectors are sharply defined, with structures terminating or turning along grid lines and no comparable features continuing beyond them.

sec.title: 3.1.3. Eastern Istrian Land Division (Grid 3)
sec.p: The most significant new result of the regional analysis is the identification of a land division system in eastern Istria (Figure 6 and Figure 7), interpreted as Roman on the basis of its morphology, spatial coherence and correspondence with the Roman centurial module. The ALS dataset revealed a coherent network of linear features corresponding to a grid composed of centuriae measuring approximately 706 × 706 m. The reconstructed grid has an orientation of 20°. A total of 23 centuriae can be reconstructed along its north–south axis, corresponding to more than 16 km, while its east–west extent reaches approximately 11.5 km. The grid maintains a consistent orientation throughout this extent. Its difference in orientation from the main Istrian grid therefore represents a consistent angular offset between two coherent networks, rather than a progressively increasing deviation within a single grid.

The identified remains extend across the eastern part of the Istrian Peninsula in the Labin region. The land division stretches from the area of Sveti Lovreč Labinski in the south to Štrmac, north of Labin. The Eastern Istrian land division occupies a geographically distinct territory of the peninsula, delimited on several sides by natural features. The Adriatic coast defines its eastern and southern sides, while Raša Bay and the course of the Raša River form a clear western boundary. In several locations, particularly north of Rabac, preserved limites extend almost to the shoreline. Only to the north is there no comparable topographic boundary, and the reconstructed extent of the system is therefore defined by the northernmost preserved limites in the vicinity of Štrmac, north of Labin. The carbonate/karstic terrain continues north of these remains and preserves numerous dry stone boundaries and other traces of historical land use. However, no further limites attributable to the Eastern Istrian grid were identified in this area.

Unlike in the Istrian land division (Grid 2), where limites remain clearly legible and are well preserved even in cultivated areas, all currently identified remains of the Eastern Istrian grid lie in areas that are not cultivated today. They survive in forest or maquis on very stony karst terrain, with shallow, poor soils or exposed rock, and appear as slight differences in height that would be difficult to recognise without ALS. In almost all cases, the modern cadastral layout does not follow the orientation of the identified grid, in contrast to parts of the Istrian land division, where the Roman orientation remains legible in many present-day parcel boundaries. Although preservation is less extensive than in the Istrian land division, the surviving structures display a consistent orientation and spatial arrangement, allowing the reconstruction of a coherent Roman land division throughout the eastern part of the peninsula.

sec.title: 3.1.4. Land Division in the Vicinity of Roč (Grid 4)
sec.p: A previously undocumented concentration of built linear features was identified approximately 8 km south-east of Buzet, in the area between Ročko Polje, Forčići, Brnobići, and Lupoglav (Figure 8 and Figure 9). Here, too, the rectangular layout and the consistent spacing suggest that the Roman centurial module can be interpreted as a Roman land surveying system. The features appear in the ALS dataset as positive-relief structures and form a consistent orthogonal arrangement. In several places, later dry stone walls are superimposed on the limites of the Roč land division without following their orientation. These later walls retain more clearly defined wall faces, whereas the underlying limites appear in ALS as flattened, undulating linear features. This superposition allows the relative stratigraphy of the built structures to be read, revealing successive phases of historical land use: the older land division organised according to the 20 × 20 actus module and the subsequent reorganisation of space through boundaries laid out independently of that grid.

The distribution of limites permits the reconstruction of a grid composed of centuriae measuring approximately 706 × 706 m and oriented at 38.8°. Approximately ten centuriae can be reconstructed within the identified area, covering about 5 km2. Their regular arrangement and correspondence with a 20 × 20 actus module support their interpretation as a Roman land division.

sec.title: 3.2. Centuriae and the Remains of Agricultural Use
sec.p: The remnants of the boundaries of the Roman land division are sometimes referred to as a ‘skeleton’, since traces of Roman land use within the centuriae are usually no longer evident. However, a systematic analysis of the ALS data shows that there are various remains of Roman land use preserved alongside the eastern Istrian coast. The case study area in this section covers approximately 15 km of coastline to the northeast of Medulin (Figure 1), between the village of Ližnjan and Krnica Bay. To ensure clear identification, the site names are based on the Croatian base map (HOK), although some toponyms may have different local names to those used on official maps. This region was chosen for several reasons. It is an almost entirely forested area with few small settlements or areas used for agriculture. Agriculture in this part of Istria must have ceased by the early modern period at the latest. This reflects the general depopulation of Istria and can also be seen on old maps, which show no settlements or agricultural land on the immediate eastern coast of Istria (e.g., [72]). The ALS data also shows that there is little overlap between the remains of the land use from different historical periods, with the number of presumed Roman remains outnumbering those from more modern periods. Furthermore, the case study area contains a wide variety of visible traces of Roman land use that can be readily compared with and interpreted considering previously published findings. Interpreting the approximately 70 centuriae revealed around 1000 individual linear or circular structures, which can be divided into two groups: the boundaries of the centuriae and internal subdivisions, as well as stone piles probably used to construct some of these boundaries.

Overall, there are slight variations in the survey grid, in terms of both the size of the individual centuriae and the layout of the grid. Although each centuria covers an area of approximately 50 ha and follows a main grid, the lengths and widths of this grid vary between 702 and 710 m. The remains of the dry stone walls used as boundary markers adapt to the topography and follow the contours of the terrain. This is particularly evident in the easternmost coastal areas, where expanses of more than 50 ha were consolidated; the individual boundaries of the centuriae were either not constructed, or adapted completely to the terrain, thereby deviating from the original surveying system. This approach, in which adaptations are made regarding the orientation of land surveying due to the natura loci, is commonly known [73].

The internal divisions of centuriae and remains of use for agricultural purposes also show great diversity. Different internal divisions in Istria have been confirmed since, at the very least, the analysis of ALS data from the region on the northern side of the Lim Channel [9], see also [70]. Similarly, the basic subdivisions of centuriae on the east coast of Istria are visible through horizontally or vertically oriented dry stone walls arranged in different patterns. A centuria may be divided in half, into thirds, or into quarters (Figure 10), after which the individual sections often become further subdivided into smaller oblong or square land plots.

In addition to traces of centuriae subdivisions, the remains of small-scale grids built using dry stone technique have also been preserved (Figure 11). In order to determine the size and orientation of the individual cells, the boundary lines of those grid cells that were either fully or partially preserved were digitised and subjected to statistical analysis. Out of a total of 104 lines, the lengths—apart from one outlier of 25 m and two of 48 m—had a mean of 35.72 metres (standard deviation: 3.22). Around half of all grid edges measured between 34 and 36 m. Their mean orientation is 16.87° and 106.87° respectively, which in both cases deviates by approximately 1° from the orientation of the centuriation (see Grid 2 in Table 3). In the absence of a known name, we will refer to it as the actus grid, since its regular units are closely aligned with the Roman actus, which measures approximately 35.52 m. This type of Roman agricultural land use remains is already known from other parts of Istria. Examples of the actus grid, originally named ‘grid-shaped parcelling’, have been found in the Medulin Bay region and on the island of Veli Brijun [37]. The shallow linear banks represent most likely the heavily eroded remains of former dry stone walls, preserved in micro-relief as low banks. The banks are up to 4 m wide and form a regular grid with square cells.

There are currently no other known comparable examples in Istria apart from the Barbariga region, which lies almost 20 km north-west of Pula. The Barbariga area features a small-scale grid, with each unit measuring approximately 75 m in length and 37–42 m in width (1 × 2 actus) (Figure 12). At its western boundary, the grid adjoins the principal limites of a centuria. Around 50 stone piles showing the same alignment as the grid itself were documented to the east of the actus grid. These remains are located amongst the extensive evidence of the Roman land surveying system. In this part of Istria, this system is also characterised by numerous roads running between the double centuriae boundaries.

Stone piles, as in the area of Barbariga, are one further category of remains that probably relate to Roman land use (Figure 13). Their layout resembles the actus grids; however, their mean distance is with 39.5 m slightly larger. Almost 400 stone piles have been documented along the east coast of Istria, between the port of Krnica and Budava Bay, though mainly within the municipality of Peruški (Figure 3). However, this number does not represent the total figure, as only the stone piles that were clearly identifiable in the archaeological remote sensing data were included. The stone piles are so dense that the local area has been given the name ‘dense stone piles’ (Croatian: guste gromače) and they have been included on the Croatian topographical map. Even though some of the stone piles are not of Roman origin, but instead prehistoric graves [see [74] for the Peruški region and [75] for the Barbariga region], and not all of them are arranged in a discernible pattern, physical connections to other remains of Roman land use, such as the land division, can be identified in many areas of the case study.

The first known aerial photograph, published by Bradford [1] (Figure 41), clearly shows the stone piles and dry stone walls amidst the dense vegetation. Whilst the dry stone walls were interpreted as limites of the centuriatio, the multiple piles of stones with diameters of 20 m were described by Bradford as ‘remains of large piles of stones cleared from the surface’ [1]. Bradford saw a clear relation to the remains of the Roman centuriatio, as the stone piles are in a regular layout parallel to the walls. He, therefore, dated them to be of Roman origin with potential re-use during later times. Almost 50 years later, R. Matijašić [67] published his research on stone piles in the same area, noting that many of the distances between individual cairns corresponded to Roman units of measurement such as the actus. He therefore also argued for the Roman origin of both the dry stone walls and stone piles. This particularly applies to the areas shown in Figure 13, which are located between the two green-marked actus grids within the centuriatio. Attempting to connect the stone piles with lines to form an actus grid reveals a mean distance of 85.83 m between them. However, this only applies to stone piles whose relative positions form a square grid. Stone piles in the north-eastern area appear to follow the orientation of the centuriatio but have different distances between them.

A field visit to the stone piles in the Peruški region in 2021 served two purposes. Firstly, the aim was to document the stone piles through further photographic recordings. The second aim was to determine whether the stone piles were connected to the local production of lime, for which the region was renowned until a few decades ago [76]. However, according to local experts, this is not the case, as fresh stone is used for lime production. Prolonged storage, as seen with the documented stone piles, causes the stone to change colour, meaning the desired white colour of the lime cannot be achieved.

sec.title: 4.1. Defining the Extent of the Centuriated Landscapes
sec.p: As outlined in Section 2.2 of the methodology, the interpretation process was iterative, involving the reconstruction of provisional centuriatio grids from previously mapped limites. These provisional grids provided a spatial reference for revisiting apparent gaps and locating faint remains that had been overlooked during the initial mapping process. Identification continued to depend on the same morphological criteria, and dry stone walls were not incorporated based solely on their alignment with projected boundaries. These additions supplemented the networks established during the initial mapping process but did not alter the extent or interpretation of the reconstructed land divisions as Roman.

The mapping of securely identified linear structures across the integrated transnational ALS dataset allowed four land division systems to be reconstructed on the basis of their orientation, spacing, and spatial distribution. Our interpretation as a Roman land-surveying system is based on their morphology, spatial coherence and correspondence with the Roman centurial module. The proposed extent of each system was defined primarily by the outermost reliably identified limites and then assessed in relation to the surrounding landscape. Such comparisons cannot establish the original extent of the centuriated areas with certainty, but they help assess whether the termination of the identified limites corresponds with broader changes in the landscape or with areas in which no comparable features occur. It is important, however, not to equate the proposed extent of the centuriated systems with the complete agri of the communities with which they may have been associated. An ager could include both lands divided and allotted to individuals and undivided land, or ager insolutus, administered by the community. The reconstructions presented here therefore concern the probable extent of the centuriated landscapes rather than the full extent of the associated territories. The gaps between neighbouring land divisions cannot be assigned to particular communities on the basis of the mapped grids alone. These areas may have belonged to a community associated with one of the neighbouring land divisions or to another community whose territory is not represented by an identified grid. Establishing their territorial affiliation requires additional evidence, such as boundary stones, inscriptions and historical sources, considered alongside the archaeological and landscape evidence.

Comparison with harmonised pedological datasets from Italy [77], Slovenia [78], and the geological map of Croatia at 1:300,000 [79] reveals a consistent regional pattern (Figure 14). The original mapping units were reclassified according to their lithological and parent material descriptions into four broad terrain categories: carbonate/karstic, flysch, mixed carbonate–clastic, and other. The mapped limites of all four land divisions are overwhelmingly concentrated in carbonate and karstic landscapes, whereas no limites were identified in flysch areas. This contrast cannot be reduced to soil or substrate type alone. Within the study area, flysch commonly forms strongly dissected hilly terrain composed of steep slopes, narrow ridges, and valleys, much of it subsequently reshaped by agricultural terracing. Čučković and Fovet [5] observed a similar pattern north of the Mirna, where traces of the main Istrian grid occur on the limestone plateau but are absent from the intervening flysch zone. They proposed that this absence may reflect the destruction of earlier boundaries through erosion, terracing, and later cultivation, while leaving open the possibility that the flysch terrain was never incorporated into the centuriated area. The recurrence of this pattern across all four systems strengthens the observed association between the mapped land divisions and carbonate landscapes, but it does not resolve whether the absence of limites in flysch areas reflects original exclusion or differential preservation.

Across the Slovenian Kras, the coastal Karst of Friuli-Venezia Giulia and much of Istria, stone was readily available, and land boundaries were commonly materialised as dry stone structures. Even where deep terra rossa developed, cultivation took place within a broader karstic environment in which stone remained abundant. The gap between the main Istrian and Eastern Istrian land divisions, and the area north of the Eastern Istrian grid, preserve numerous dry stone boundaries and other traces of historical land use. Their survival suggests that the absence of Roman land division remains in these areas is unlikely to result simply from later destruction. The proposed extents are therefore more securely supported here than along the flysch margins between the Tergeste and main Istrian systems, where erosion, terracing and later cultivation may have removed earlier boundaries.

sec.title: 4.2. The Tergeste Land Division (Grid 1) and Grid 4: Spatial Extent and Territorial Context
sec.p: The integrated reconstruction of the Tergeste land division brings together features previously documented in the Slovenian and Italian Karst [68,69] and newly identified coastal limites, demonstrating that they belong to a single system extending across the present-day border. All securely identified limites associated with this system occur within the carbonate landscapes of the Karst plateau, while no comparable features have been identified in the adjoining flysch areas (Figure 14). It therefore remains uncertain whether the apparent termination of the system towards the east and south-east reflects its original extent or the poorer preservation of built boundaries within the steep, erosion-prone, and extensively terraced flysch landscape.

Towards the north-west, the proposed extent of the Tergeste system is tentatively drawn to the edge of the Karst plateau. The only possible continuation towards Monfalcone is the isolated feature noted above. Beyond the plateau lies the adjoining alluvial plain. Several Roman land division grids have been proposed for the Aquileian plain, including the generally accepted 20 × 20 actus ‘classical’ grid, although the reconstruction and relationship of the different grids remain debated [80]. Any spatial relationship between the Tergeste land division and these grids remains unclear.

South-east of the Tergeste system, Grid 4 occupies the area in the vicinity of Roč, generally identified with Roman Rotium. Its orientation differs from that of the Tergeste land division by approximately 3°. This relatively small difference is noteworthy, but the two land divisions are spatially discontinuous, and similarity in orientation alone cannot establish a chronological or administrative relationship between them.

The territorial affiliation of the Buzet–Roč area has long been debated. Girardi Jurkić and Džin [81] placed Buzet, identified with Roman Piquentum, and Roč within the ager of Tergeste, as part of a broader reconstruction in which the Tergestine territory extended southwards to the Mirna and included much of northern Istria. The identification of the main Istrian grid north of the Mirna and as far as the Dragonja makes the western part of this broad territorial reconstruction difficult to maintain, but it has no direct bearing on the specific affiliation of the Buzet–Roč area. A recent synthesis of the archaeological and historical evidence from the Buzeština likewise emphasises the uncertainty surrounding the legal status of Piquentum and Rotium and their relationship with Tergeste [82]. Grid 4 cannot, by itself, confirm or disprove the inclusion of the Buzet–Roč area within the territory of Tergeste.

The epigraphic evidence from the Buzet–Roč area reflects the continued visibility of indigenous personal names among communities previously thought to lie outside the colonial agri [83]. The identification of a regular Roman land division in the same area complicates, rather than overturns, this interpretation. It shows that Roman surveying, and possibly land allotment, was undertaken in an area where a substantial indigenous population remained visible. In the absence of chronological evidence for the limites, it remains uncertain whether the land division was connected with the organisation of land around Piquentum or Rotium, with a phase in which the area was administratively associated with Tergeste, or with another episode of Roman territorial reorganisation.

sec.title: 4.3. The Main Istrian Land Division (Grid 2): Extent and Patterns of Materialisation
sec.p: The mapped limites of the main Istrian grid (Grid 2), extending from southern Istria to the Dragonja River, share the same orientation and spacing, supporting their interpretation as elements of a single coherent land division traditionally associated with Pola and Parentium. The Mirna River was traditionally regarded as the northern limit of the known Istrian centuriatio, a position reflected in the reconstructions of Marchiori [35] and Bulić [27]. Bernardini and Vinci [36] first challenged this interpretation by identifying several fossil linear features near Oprtalj whose orientation and position correspond with the established Istrian grid. Čučković and Fovet [5] subsequently mapped a much broader distribution of preserved limites across the area between the Mirna and Dragonja rivers. The present analysis confirms that these remains form part of the main Istrian land division and reconstructs its continuation to the Dragonja River on the basis of securely identified physical features. The much wider projected network proposed by Bernardini and Vinci, however, is not supported by the distribution of preserved limites identified in the present ALS analysis.

At its northern end, the Istrian land division can be followed as far as the Dragonja River but not securely identified limites attributable either to this grid or to the Tergeste land division have been recognised between the Dragonja River and Rižana River. This gap corresponds largely to the dissected and extensively terraced flysch landscape discussed above (Figure 14). Given its hilly character and the absence of identifiable limites, we consider it unlikely that this area was ever centuriated. However, we cannot rule out the possibility that erosion, terracing and later cultivation have removed earlier boundaries. The gap is nevertheless historically significant because Aegida, generally located in the area of modern Koper, lay within this intervening zone. Pliny lists Aegida as an oppidum civium Romanorum [84], although this designation does not establish its precise juridical status. Matijašić [85] argued that it possessed a degree of self-government while remaining subordinate to Tergeste in certain rights and obligations. Aegida may nevertheless have possessed an organised territory, although no centuriated land division can presently be attributed securely to the community.

The eastern extent of the main Istrian grid is less clearly defined. In the reconstructions of Marchiori [35] and Bulić [27], the main grid was largely confined to the area west of the eastern end of the Limska draga. The present mapping identifies a limited number of remains farther east. Several limites corresponding securely with the grid occur north of Svetvinčenat, near Maružini, while a small but well-preserved group of adjoining centuriae, including internal divisions, survives between Bokordići and Šajini. Their limited and discontinuous distribution, however, does not permit the eastern boundary of the land division to be reconstructed with certainty or explain why the physical materialisation of the grid becomes so restricted in this area.

Beyond these remains lies a broad zone separating the main Istrian grid from the newly identified eastern land division (Grid 3). Although this part of the peninsula differs from the deep terra rossa landscapes farther west and south, particularly through its more pronounced karstic microrelief and greater density of dolines, these conditions alone do not explain the absence of identifiable built limites. Numerous dry stone boundaries and other traces of historical land use remain clearly visible between the dolines, demonstrating that the earlier organisation of the landscape has not simply been erased. None of these features forms a coherent network corresponding with the orientation and spacing of the main grid. The gap therefore appears to represent an area that was not incorporated into the physically materialised land division, rather than merely an area of poor archaeological preservation. This pattern is compatible with the hypothesis that, following the division and assignment of the colonial territories, some indigenous communities were displaced towards, or remained concentrated within, the central and peripheral parts of the peninsula [86], but it provides no direct evidence for such population movements or settlement patterns.

The exceptional preservation of the main Istrian grid is most apparent in southern Istria. South of an approximate line connecting Rovinj on the western coast with Rakalj on the eastern coast and apart from the Premantura Peninsula, a continuous network of built limites defines adjoining centuriae across almost the entire peninsula, from coast to coast. Because the grid is so extensive and continuously materialised in southern Istria, abrupt gaps within it cannot automatically be attributed to later destruction.

North of this continuously built southern sector, the materialisation of the grid becomes more spatially differentiated (Figure 15). Between the hilltop of Mulem in the south and the village of Bubani in the north, a dense network of built limites and internal divisions occupies a sharply defined strip exactly five centuriae wide and more than ten centuriae long. Along both sides of this strip, individual structures terminate or turn at right angles, showing that their construction was confined to the area between these boundaries and did not originally continue into the adjoining landscape (Figure 16).

The opposite pattern occurs in the hinterland of Parentium. Between Dračevac in the south and Milanezi in the north, a sharply defined strip exactly five centuriae wide contains no built limites, although the same grid is physically materialised in the surrounding areas. The contrast between the unbuilt strip and the surrounding built sectors occurs within comparable karstic terrain, with no systematic difference in vegetation cover. No evidence of recent disturbance sufficient to explain the absence of built limites was identified. Other traces of historical land use remain clearly visible in ALS within both the unbuilt strip and the neighbouring built sector. Recent disturbance, vegetation differences and inadequate visibility in ALS therefore do not provide sufficient explanations for the contrast, supporting its interpretation as a difference in the physical materialisation of the grid.

The clearly defined extent of both the built and unbuilt strips indicates that the geometric survey and the construction of boundary features were distinct processes, and that the physical materialisation of the grid may have been organised in larger spatial units. That both strips are exactly five centuriae wide may be significant, although any relationship with quintarii or another higher-order organisation of the centuriated landscape requires further examination.

sec.title: 4.4. The Eastern Istrian Land Division (Grid 3): Relationship with the Main Istrian Grid 2 and Territorial Context
sec.p: The identification of a previously unknown land division in eastern Istria (Grid 3) is the most significant new result of the present study (Figure 6). Its relationship with the main Istrian grid remains uncertain. Their orientations differ by only approximately 2°, and their closest spatial correspondence occurs in the south, where the eastern grid near Sveti Lovreč Labinski approaches the main Istrian grid in the area of Rakalj. This raises the possibility that one survey was laid out with reference to the other. At the same time, the eastern grid constitutes a clearly separate land division, occupying a distinct part of the peninsula, east of the Raša River and separated from the main grid across most of its extent by the broad zone without identifiable built limites described above. No physical junction between the two grids can be identified, as they are separated by the Raša Channel and River.

The reconstructed grid extends northwards into the area of Alvona but ends well south of Flanona, indicating a closer spatial relationship with the former. Both settlements are generally treated as Roman municipia of northern Liburnia, east of the Raša River and outside Regio X Venetia et Histria [83,87]. The distribution of the mapped limites corresponds more closely with the territory around Alvona, although this alone does not demonstrate that the grid belonged to its territory. Grid 3 should therefore be considered within the territorial context of northern Liburnia rather than simply as an extension of the Pola–Parentium land division. Since the eastern land division cannot presently be dated, it remains uncertain whether this similarity reflects contemporary surveys, one survey laid out with reference to the other, or separate episodes of Roman territorial organisation.

The four reconstructed land divisions show considerable differences in their extent and in the way they were physically materialised. Within the main Istrian grid, the geometric survey continues across areas with very different degrees of physical materialisation, from densely built sectors to areas with few or no constructed boundaries. The reconstructed centuriated areas also need not correspond to the full territories of the colonies or other communities with which they were associated. While the discussion so far has considered these questions on a regional scale, the following section examines the surviving limites, internal divisions, and plots in greater detail.

sec.title: 4.5. Roman Land Use in Historical Context of Istria
sec.p: Any historical period that has endured long enough to leave a lasting mark on the landscape has created its own distinctive patterns. This applies to prehistoric times, but even more so to the period of Roman rule. The most defining feature of the Istrian landscape, and that of other regions at the time, is the extensive land division. Following the establishment of the colonies of Pola and Parentium, a comprehensive land organisation process began. The land allocations carried out during this process [88] have left their mark in the form of the internal divisions of the centuriae. The east coast of Istria, with its abundance of such remains (altogether more than 500 features), demonstrates that the surveying was not merely carried out pro forma but was followed by actual agricultural use. Evidence of comparable divisions is rarely found [88], as they were seldom the focus of study and as the available data from other regions rarely revealed any traces of them.

In the ALS data from Istria, various rectangular boundaries, the actus grid and numerous stone piles can be identified. The knowledge of the Roman actus grid in the Medulin Bay region and on the island of Veli Brijun [37] supports the comparable dating of remains from the eastern Istrian coast. This is reinforced by the shared Roman units of measurement and the spatial alignment of the centuriatio limites and their subdivisions with the actus grid and stone piles (Figure 12 and Figure 13). The Roman dating of the stone piles, as previously proposed by Bradford [1] and Matijašić [67], appears to be supported by the new findings. Regarding their interpretation, it is conceivable that, whilst the stone piles were being built up, the land was cleared and the soil prepared, during which process loose stones were piled up into heaps. It is also possible that some of the stone piles were used as burial mounds at different times. For the stone piles shown in Figure 13, which lie between the two green-marked actus grids within the centuriatio and within a square grid with an average spacing of 85.83 m (see Section 3.2), another interpretation seems probable. Given their proximity to the incomplete actus grids, their arrangement and orientation, and their uniform size, they could also be interpreted as building material for the actus grid or other internal subdivisions. The unfinished actus grid at Barbariga is also flanked by piles of prepared stones (Figure 13). Further investigation into this topic is already planned (see below).

While these remains all bear witness to the agricultural use of the centuriae, they do not necessarily need to be interpreted as agricultural areas serving the needs of small households. Of the five sites in the far south-east of the municipality of Marčana where Matijašić [67] presumed villae rusticae, no traces are discernible in the ALS data. In contrast, data from at least two other locations (Velika Lokva and Blatina) reveal the remains of small villas. When investigating Roman land use in an agricultural context, research generally assumes that identifying the location of villae rusticae can provide new insights. However, this overlooks the fact that land use, whether in the form of land division, resource extraction, agriculture or habitation, is extremely complex in political, economic and historical terms. Various economic interests lie between the political and legal decision to carry out a centuriatio and the establishment of the villae rusticae, i.e., the small, independent estates. One example is the economic interests of the large Roman estates, the so-called villae maritimae.

The diversity of the newly discovered physical remains of land use provides some evidence to suggest that the construction effort, costs, corresponding transport and sales infrastructure, and time required to generate profit from the yields represented a long-term investment. This raises the question of whether large-scale agricultural production for profit in the context of 1st and 2nd century villae maritimae was limited solely to the west coast and whether some of the newly documented evidence of land use suggests otherwise. Currently, there is no evidence of this on the east coast of Istria, although targeted research could transform our understanding of the area.

The Late Republic and Early Imperial periods were characterised by a significant increase in investment in Istria. This is evident in the growth of towns, land division and the first appearance of the large Roman estates (summary in [89]). Tassaux refers to the owners of the villae maritimae in Histria simply as ‘les milliardaires de l’Adriatique romaine’ [90]. The term can be interpreted in two different ways. Firstly, it refers to a wealthy social class that took advantage of the intertwining of politics and economics in the new border regions. Starac [25] sees practical economic advantages in the change in the border of Histria and the closer ties with the Italian peninsula, which primarily benefited the narrow elite circle around the Emperor Augustus. But the term also encompasses the ability of the Roman upper class to finance luxurious living spaces, as well as to invest the required capital within their own estates in major economic sectors of that time [91]. They mark a brief period of prosperity, which Kehoe [92] describes for Italy as perhaps the greatest boom in agriculture during the last two centuries BC and first century AD.

What is described for Italy also applies to Istria, albeit somewhat delayed. The fact that Istria actually practiced a systematic agricultural production in Roman times can also be deduced from the fact that olive oil from Istria was known in other regions of the Roman Empire, which is evident from the praising mentions, e.g., by Pliny the Elder or Martial [26]. Recent discoveries, based on archaeological remote sensing, seem to confirm the first physical evidence of large-scale agriculture in Istria, in the form of orchards/nurseries and actus grids, managed by villae maritimae [37].

To date, the actus grid has only been identified in connection with large-scale agriculture, involving sometimes extensively laid-out planting pits. The Barbariga region is perhaps the best example of this, being home to the largest Roman production facility in Istria [26], a villa maritima [26], planting pits [37], and a small-scale grid with stone piles situated close together (Figure 12). On the other hand, this presumed relationship may simply reflect the current state of research, as actus grids may have been a common and widely used form of cultivation in the past. The Roman preference for uniform, rectangular spatial patterns is evident in many areas of agriculture [93,94].

In this context, the new results on Roman surveying of Istria build a coherent database ready for detailed research. Some of these questions will be investigated as part of the research project ‘PROFIT: Profitable Roman estates on the Istrian shores’ (2026–2029), as the study presented here focuses generally on the potential of archaeological remote sensing in the northern Adriatic coastal region. Since the study area covers 4000 km2 and encompasses a variety of landscapes, including agricultural land with modern dry stone walls overlaying Roman boundaries and the densely vegetated eastern coast of Istria, no fieldwork is involved in the study. As previously mentioned, access to many archaeological remains on the eastern coast, including stone piles, is currently limited. For this reason, all fieldwork must be planned and carried out systematically within a broader research context.
