The PROFIT project provides such a framework and will incorporate on-site documentation and modelling the construction costs of dry stone walls, with a particular focus on presumed Roman stone piles [95]. Another area of focus will be the further investigation of Roman agricultural remains. The project involves the spatial extent of large-scale agriculture and the nature of this agricultural production, using palynological, pollen and sediment DNA analysis. Selected stone piles, internal divisions and limites of the centuriae will be dated using optically stimulated luminescence. This will provide the first absolute chronological evidence of the evolution and development of the centuriated landscape and the agricultural remains in Istria. This may also provide clues as to whether the incomplete actus grids originated from some investors failing to take advantage of the trend in time. The results will open new possibilities for the understanding of economic activities in the profit-oriented economy of the villae maritimae. Understanding their complexity is also the best way to discuss the political and cultural changes that accompanied the establishment of Roman Histria within a broader context.

sec.title: 4.6. Strengths and Limitations of the Approach
sec.p: Combining nationwide laser scans from three neighbouring countries facilitates cross-border archaeological work. Access to the classified point clouds has enabled the creation of a digital terrain model that meets archaeological requirements, improving the interpretation of the data for archaeological purposes. The digital feature model, which displays not only the relief but also buildings and wall structures, focuses on archaeological interest and enhances the identification of features relevant to archaeological interpretation. However, compromises had to be made. We had carried out tests on a smaller section of the Croatian dataset in eastern Istria in this regard. While the parameters typically used for our archaeologically motivated classifications [15,55] produced a slightly less noisy feature model, the archaeological benefit was for our research question minimal. Still, due to the sheer volume of data and the heterogeneity of the landscapes, it was impossible to calculate a new classification of the point data based on archaeological criteria. Overcoming these restrictions would have enhanced the quality of interpretation in certain regions and therefore remains desirable.

The Specific Combined Visualisation for Archaeological Topography (CVAT) combines the most important visualisations used in archaeological prospecting into a single image, making it particularly well suited to interpretations where only one visualisation can be used for technical reasons. An additional layer containing elevation data would be useful for interpretation, for example, to measure the stone pile heights, but this could not be implemented for national legal reasons. Consequently, it is not possible to derive terrain profiles from the data. This is a frequently used method in the archaeological interpretation of terrain models as it helps to distinguish between terraces and ramparts or determine whether break lines in the terrain are accompanied by a rampart.

Due to the extensive nature of our analysis, which covered an area of over 4000 km2, the archaeological interpretation of the data also required adaptation. A stratigraphic, diachronic interpretation of the ALS-based visualisations in the context of landscape archaeology would have required excessive effort. For this reason, this study does not present landscape archaeology but rather a targeted analysis of large-scale prospection data that provides a foundation for future landscape archaeological research. The dataset has the potential for further detailed diachronous interpretations, as stratigraphies can be deduced from the overlap of dry stone walls, paths, terraces, lime kilns and material extraction sites.

The broader implications for understanding of the Istrian landscape stem from the fact that our knowledge is strongly impacted by the current state of research. An example of this can be seen in the internal division of the centuriae. Unlike research into Roman centuriatio, studies of the agricultural use of centuriae in Istria have, so far, been largely overlooked. Several factors have contributed to this. Until 15 years ago, research of land divisions could only be conducted using aerial photographs, which revealed the remains only in areas under intensive agricultural use. While the Roman limites are often still visible in those regions today, this is not the case for the remains of dry stone walls, which were originally used to subdivide the centuriae. In many places these have not survived centuries of agricultural activity, as plots were cleared of old or now useless stone piles or dry stone walls to make way for arable farming. Although forested areas are an exception to this rule, they were only recognised as valuable research areas after the advent of ALS. Furthermore, archaeological research has traditionally focused on sites and artefacts, considering dry stone walls to be non-site areas as it was impossible to date them without accompanying finds. However, archaeological finds represent only one type of available archaeological source. Past cultures are manifested not only in archaeological sites and finds but also in every regional cultural tradition and landscape. This can take the form of myths, slightly altered geographical names (such as Roman Histria and modern-day Istria), or the adapted reuse of past infrastructure. In this way, the memory of regional history is kept alive. For this reason, a broad-scale interpretation of landscape features can provide further insights. To achieve this, however, it is necessary to shift the focus away from individual monuments or sites and consider all traces of the Roman era as components of the Roman landscape.

sec.title: 5. Conclusions
sec.p: The integration of ALS datasets from Italy, Slovenia, and Croatia enabled research on four Roman land divisions across the Gulf of Trieste and the Istrian Peninsula within a single geographical framework. This demonstrates the value of the harmonised CFVGS-CVAT, which facilitates archaeological research by overcoming the constraints of national borders. Furthermore, the model balances differences in the national datasets, enabling it to be used directly. Consequently, the focus can be placed on areas that are crucial to research, such as geographical and cultural regions that constitute a historical unity and are far more relevant for archaeological research than modern political borders.

The analysis brings together remains of the Tergeste land division previously studied separately on either side of the modern border, confirms the continuation of the main Istrian grid to the Dragonja River, and identifies previously unrecognised land divisions in eastern Istria and in the Buzet–Roč area. Their differing extents, the substantial gaps between them, and the marked variation in their physical materialisation demonstrate that Roman land division across the region was neither spatially continuous nor uniformly implemented. They also show that the preserved extent of a centuriated landscape cannot be equated directly with the complete territory of the community with which it may have been associated.

These results do not replace the substantial historiography of Roman Istria and the northern Adriatic but add a new layer of spatial evidence to the written, epigraphic, archaeological, and geographical data already available. The transnational extent of the Tergeste land division, the continuation of the main Istrian grid north of the Mirna River, and the identification of a separate land division east of the Raša River all provide grounds for questioning long-standing territorial and administrative models. At the same time, the evidence does not provide simple alternatives to these models, since the chronology and territorial affiliation of several of the reconstructed land divisions require further studies.

A centuriated landscape encompasses not only the boundaries of land divisions but also land use patterns. Analysing the subdivisions within individual centuriae provided a unique insight into their former use. Alongside the various rectangular boundaries, evidence of agricultural land use was found in the form of small-scale grids and numerous stone piles, offering insight into former land use practices.

The present study has focused primarily on ALS evidence, placing the reconstructed land divisions and other land use remains within their broader geographical and historical contexts. Further research into the historical and economic background of the centuriated landscape is required. Investigating the history of Roman territories in Histria would require the systematic integration of additional evidence, including boundary stones and inscriptions, as well as indigenous and Roman settlement patterns and road networks. The relative and absolute dating of the land divisions across the Gulf of Trieste and the Istrian Peninsula, their subdivisions and other land use remains, as well as research into Roman agricultural practices, will provide new key data on the spatial and temporal development of Roman Histria. Examining the relationships between land division, land allotment, settlement, economic organisation and civic territory in closer detail is also a valuable research area. Therefore, the importance of integrated national and transnational ALS datasets lies not only in identifying additional limites or grids but also in providing a new evidential layer through which established interpretations can be reconsidered and the histories of these landscapes can be more fully reconstructed.
